history_of_present_illness: Patients with Gangosa are rarely observed before the full development of mutilating ulcerations. In early cases, a patch of membrane may appear in the region of the soft palate, which rapidly becomes honeycombed. Within three or four days, a deep ulcer surrounded by marked congestion develops underneath. The ulcerating process advances rapidly, destroying both bone and soft tissues, extending from within outward to create a funnel-shaped loss of tissue. It advances upward and forward, destroying the nasal septum and the structures forming the tip of the nose, leaving the upper lip as the lower border of the external opening. The active process tends to become quiescent in one or two years, resulting in extensive tissue loss with cicatricial borders; however, active ulceration may occasionally recur after a period of quiescence. The frequent perforation of the hard palate gives patients a characteristic nasal or muffled voice. During active ulceration, a malodorous sero-purulent discharge is present. Despite the destructive lesions, patients typically suffer little impairment of general health. Similar ulcers may also occur on the extremities.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Gangosa was first reported in 1828 by a Spanish Commission in the Ladrone Islands (now Marianas), where it was noted for the muffled character of the voice. The disease is very prevalent in Guam and is also found in other islands of the Caroline group, Fiji, Dominica (West Indies), the Philippines, and Ceylon. Its etiology is primarily debated between being a sequel of yaws or syphilis. The disease responds to antisyphilitic treatment, but this is not considered definitive proof of syphilitic origin, as yaws also responds similarly. Gangosa cases show a considerable percentage of positive Wassermann reactions (105 positives in 281 cases), although 100% positivity is found in yaws cases and 46% in those with a history of yaws. Arguments against a syphilitic nature include the absence of congenital or acquired syphilis in the native populations of Guam, with no reported Hutchinson’s teeth or interstitial keratitis. A positive luetin reaction has been obtained in 253 out of 369 gangosa cases. However, syphilitic and yaws antigens appear to be reciprocal, making these tests inconclusive for differentiation. Evidence supporting yaws as the etiology includes 205 out of 315 gangosa cases showing yaws scars, and yaws treponemata found in smears from active ulcerations following yaws in children. If gangosa is a sequel of yaws, then the same epidemiological factors that apply to yaws are also relevant to gangosa.
physical_exam: Physical findings are dominated by mutilating ulcerations, particularly in the nasopharyngeal region and face. Initial manifestations can include a patch of membrane on the soft palate. The ulceration rapidly destroys cartilage and bone, extending from within outward, resulting in a funnel-shaped loss of tissue. It progresses upward and forward, causing destruction of the nasal septum and the structures forming the tip of the nose, leaving the upper lip as the lower border of the external opening. The characteristic muffled or nasal voice results from the frequent perforation of the hard palate. The nasal duct is prone to attack, which can lead to involvement of the eye (observed in 21 out of 81 cases). The larynx was involved in 33 out of 81 studied cases. During active ulceration, there is a malodorous sero-purulent discharge. After one to two years, the active process typically becomes quiescent, leaving extensive tissue loss with cicatricial borders. Similar ulcers may also be observed on the extremities.
labs_and_diagnostics: Microscopic examination of sections from the ulcerating margins stained by Levaditi’s method has failed to show treponemata. However, sections stained by Giemsa’s method revealed a marked infiltration with lymphocytes and a large number of mast cells; the presence of giant cells has also been noted. Histologically, the lesions exhibit characteristics of granulomata. Blood examinations in a limited number of cases (10) showed no abnormal findings other than eosinophilia, which was equally present in unaffected individuals. A slight leucocytosis has also been reported in some cases. Diagnostic tests include a considerable percentage of positive Wassermann reactions (105 positives in 281 cases of gangosa), although similar or higher positivity is seen in yaws. A positive luetin reaction was obtained in 253 out of 369 gangosa cases, presenting as papular, pustular, or torpid types. Yaws treponemata have been found in smears from ulcerated areas in cases observed following yaws.
differential_diagnosis: Gangosa is primarily differentiated from leprosy, syphilis, and lupus vulgaris. Its more rapid course helps distinguish it from leprosy and lupus, while the patient's history aids in differentiating it from syphilis.
management_and_clinical_course: Antisyphilitic treatment has been found effective in curing these ulcerations. Mercurial injections were previously used, and more recently, salvarsan has yielded striking curative results. While local application of tincture of iodine was thought to be effective in stopping early ulcerations, its efficacy is doubtful, and immediate administration of salvarsan is advisable. Solutions of permanganate of potash are generally used to manage the offensive odor of the discharge. The active disease process typically becomes quiescent within one to two years, leading to extensive tissue loss with cicatricial borders. Although recurrences of active ulceration can occur, patients generally experience very little impairment of their general health.
